title: Trapping Nanoparticles in Nanofluidic Traps Using a Monolithic Liquid Phase-TEM Chip
content: Recent development of liquid phase transmission electron microscopy (LPTEM) has enabled the use of standard TEM systems to observe liquid samples encapsulated between two thin membranes. The main LPTEM limitations are the non-controlled liquid thickness between the membranes and the interaction between the electron beam and the sample, which can lead to radiolysis [1, 2]. The thickness limitation is due to ambient pressure giving bulging of the membranes and leads to low TEM resolution. Monolithic chips with nanochannels embedded into the membrane [3, 4] has provided few nanometers bulging compared to micrometers in traditional clamped chips systems, as nanochannels have a width of a few micrometers opposed to tens of micrometers in clamped chip membranes. The radiolysis limitation has been compensated by using more sensitive detectors, allowing imaging with a lower electron beam dose. Still, LPTEM challenges remain, such as reliably getting nanoparticles in the viewing area. One approach to overcome this problem is to use highly concentrated solutions to increase the probability of nanoparticles sticking to the membrane. However, other problems can arise from this approach such as clogging due to agglomeration. Additionally, relying on random sticking of the nanoparticles could result in a non-representative population of the original sample only imaging the most adherent subpopulation. Anyway, typically low concentration solutions are required in single particle studies, where the structure or the reactions occurring at the surface are analyzed individually for each nanoparticle.
